analysis.one_liner: Taxes 95% of large corporations' profits above their pre-2020 levels through 2026.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would tax large corporations' profits above their 2015-2019 levels at 95%, never received a hearing or vote after being referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would impose a 95% tax on the "excess profits" of large corporations — companies with at least $500 million in average annual gross receipts — meaning profits above what the company earned in 2015-2019, adjusted for inflation. It would apply to tax years starting in 2024 and end after 2026, and would cap the tax at 75% of a company's taxable income. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and the federal Treasury, if the revenue were used for public purposes; the bill's sponsors framed it as recapturing windfall profits large corporations earned as prices rose after 2020. The bill does not specify how the money would be spent.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 95% tax on profits of corporations with at least $500 million in average annual gross receipts that exceed the company's average 2015-2019 profits, adjusted for inflation.
Applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2023, and expires after tax year 2026, so it targets the post-2020 profit surge rather than creating a permanent new tax.
Broadens the definition of taxable executive pay under current law so performance bonuses for more executives cannot be deducted from corporate income.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations — most notably big retail, drug, energy, and tech companies whose post-2020 profits far exceeded pre-pandemic levels — and, indirectly, their shareholders through lower returns.

drawbacks.text: The bill taxes profits above a 2015-2019 baseline, but higher profits are not always windfalls; companies that grew legitimately during and after the pandemic would pay the tax even without price-gouging, and the bill's title notwithstanding, it does not distinguish 'excess' profits from earned growth.
The threshold is based on gross receipts ($500 million), not profits, so it reaches many mid-size companies, including ones that were barely profitable.
The tax applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2023 — profits that, at the June 2024 introduction date, were already being earned — making it effectively retroactive.
The bill says nothing about how the revenue would be used, so the money would go to general Treasury spending rather than to any specific relief for households facing higher prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea — recapturing a share of the post-2020 surge in large-corporation profits — has real public appeal, but the design is blunt: a profits-over-baseline tax punishes companies that grew for good reasons, sweeps in firms by gross receipts regardless of profitability, and reaches back to profits already earned. A narrower windfall-profits tax with a stated use for the revenue would have been easier to defend.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee after its referral on the day it was introduced, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jamaal Bowman introduced the bill on June 21, 2024, joined by Reps. Jayapal, Schakowsky, and Tlaib as cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
That was the bill's last action of record; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
It attracted only 4 cosponsors in a House of 440 voting members.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with profits far above their pre-2020 levels are better off: the tax never advanced, so nothing was imposed. Shareholders of those companies likewise keep the profits the bill would have taxed.

for.name: Jamaal Bowman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill imposing a 95% excess profits tax on large corporations.

for.name: 4 of 216 House Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Reps. Jayapal, Schakowsky, Tlaib, and one more)

against.name: Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or committee vote after it was referred to the committee.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors and cosponsors were progressive Democrats; the bill went to a committee chaired by a Republican who took no action, and no Republican supported it.

industries.industry: Large corporations (excluding real estate investment trusts, regulated investment companies, and S corporations)
industries.note: The bill would tax 95% of profits above the company's inflation-adjusted 2015-2019 average, capped at 75% of taxable income. Corporations earning far more than before 2020 would face the largest bills.
Corporate taxes are ultimately borne partly by shareholders through lower returns, so investors in large profitable companies would absorb much of the tax.
The bill broadens the rule limiting deductible executive compensation so pay to a wider set of top earners at affected companies can no longer reduce corporate taxable income.
